I write the recap within an hour, always, and I do it before I do anything else, because after an hour everybody has a slightly different meeting in their head, and the first thing that gets written down becomes the true one. It is not administration. It is the last move of the negotiation. There are three parts and I never skip any of them. What was decided. What was not decided. And the action items, with a name and a date on every single line. The middle one is the part everybody leaves out, and it is the part that saves the deal. If I write, the start date is still open because you need to speak to your team, then the open question is in front of somebody, and an open question in writing is a question that somebody will eventually answer. If I leave it out because it feels negative, it disappears, and in six weeks two companies are surprised at each other.

Most action items die for the same two reasons, and both of them are visible on the page. The first one is that nobody owns it. A task with no name on it is not a task, it is a wish, and everybody in the room quietly assumes somebody else will pick it up. The second one is that there is no date. If a line has no date, nothing about it can ever be late, and if nothing can be late, nobody is ever behind. That is why we will look into it is the most useless sentence in business English. Nobody is we, and look into it is not a verb anybody can be measured on. One more thing, and this is the one people find uncomfortable. If somebody refuses to take a deadline, write down that they refused, politely, and say when you will follow up. The refusal is information. It belongs in the recap exactly like everything else does.
